cards.q: Older study of preparing drugs and their medical uses; forerunner of pharmacology
cards.a: Materia medica

cards.q: Why materia medica could not become a true science of drug action
cards.a: No scientific principles applied; physiology, pathology and chemistry too rudimentary

cards.q: Malaria: who laid down the protocol for cinchona bark, and when
cards.a: Lind, 1765

cards.q: Johnson's 1804 advice on cinchona in fever
cards.a: Cinchona unsafe until fever subsided; large calomel doses in early stages instead

cards.q: Calomel, chemically
cards.a: Mercurous chloride

cards.q: Pre-scientific remedy recommended by Robert Boyle (1692)
cards.a: Concoctions of worms, dung, urine and moss from a dead man's skull

cards.q: Plant drugs whose medicinal use was learnt from traditional systems: list
cards.a: Opium, belladonna, ephedra, cinchona, curare, foxglove, sarpagandha, qinghaosu

cards.q: Coffee's stimulant effect first noticed through
cards.a: Behaviour of goats that frisked all night after eating coffee berries

cards.q: Deadly nightshade (Atropa belladonna) extract: use and active principle
cards.a: Dilating pupils for beauty; atropine

cards.q: Ma huang: active principle and use
cards.a: Ephedrine; used as a stimulant

cards.q: Curare: traditional use by South American indigenous people
cards.a: Paralysing animals hunted for food

cards.q: Opium: principal alkaloid and long-standing uses
cards.a: Morphine; pain relief and control of diarrhoea

cards.q: Origin of the name morphine
cards.a: Greek Morpheus, god of dreams

cards.q: Who purified morphine from opium, and in what year
cards.a: Friedrich Serturner, a young German apothecary, 1805

cards.q: What morphine purification showed
cards.a: Chemicals, not magic or vital forces, produced the effects of plant extracts

cards.q: Substances studied by early pharmacology, before synthetic chemistry
cards.a: Natural plant extracts and a few toxic chemicals (mercury, arsenic)

cards.q: Diethyl ether and nitrous oxide before their anaesthetic use
cards.a: Used socially; nitrous oxide prepared by Humphry Davy in 1799

cards.q: Amyl nitrite: year made, and why called a 'rational' drug
cards.a: 1859; angina effect predicted from its physiological actions

cards.q: Aspirin: first synthesis, rediscovery and commercial launch
cards.a: Synthesised 1853; rediscovered 1897 by Bayer; marketed 1899

cards.q: Homeopathy: founder and era
cards.a: Hahnemann, early 19th century; 'like cures like'

cards.q: Allopathy: proponent and favoured remedies
cards.a: James Gregory (1735-1821); bloodletting, emetics, purgatives

cards.q: Medical model: how it defines disease
cards.a: Derangement of normal function, defined physiologically or structurally, objectively detectable

cards.q: 'Father of pharmacology' and his era
cards.a: Oswald Schmiedeberg, late 19th century

cards.q: Schmiedeberg's disciples named in KDT8: list
cards.a: J Langley, T Frazer, P Ehrlich, AJ Clark, JJ Abel

cards.q: Rudolf Buchheim: founded the first pharmacology institute in
Pioneers of animal experiments applied to drug study (18th-19th century)
cards.a: F Magendie and Claude Bernard

cards.q: Century in which animal experiments began in pharmacology
cards.a: 18th century

cards.q: Receptor concept for chemical mediators: proposed by, year
cards.a: Langley, 1905

cards.q: Pharmacologists who took up the receptor concept after Langley
cards.a: Clark, Gaddum, Schild and others

cards.q: Ehrlich's dictum on drug action (Corpora non agunt nisi fixata)
cards.a: A drug will not work unless it is bound

cards.q: Ehrlich's 'magic bullet' phrase describes the potential of
cards.a: Antimicrobial drugs

cards.q: Ehrlich's insight into drug action
cards.a: Drug action follows ordinary chemical interactions, not vital forces

cards.q: Ehrlich's dye experiments led him to propose
cards.a: Chemical receptors that 'fixed' dyes; microbial receptors that could spare host tissue

cards.q: Arsphenamine (salvarsan): year invented and use
cards.a: 1907; used against syphilis until penicillin

cards.q: Henry Dale: main contribution
cards.a: Foundations of chemical transmission and the autonomic nervous system

cards.q: Hitchings and Elion: main contribution
cards.a: Antimetabolite principle; first effective anticancer drugs

cards.q: James Black: first drugs introduced
cards.a: First beta-adrenoceptor antagonist and first histamine H2-receptor antagonist

cards.q: William Blair-Bell: agent used for breast cancer, and city
cards.a: Lead colloid mixtures, Liverpool

cards.q: Cell theory, first structural formula, and bacteria as disease cause (dates)
cards.a: Virchow 1858; structural formula 1868; Pasteur 1878

cards.q: Gerhard Domagk: compound and year
cards.a: Prontosil, 1935; first clinically useful sulfonamide

cards.q: Effect of prontosil that launched antimicrobial chemotherapy
cards.a: Dramatically effective against streptococcal infection

cards.q: Penicillin: developed by whom, based on whose earlier work
cards.a: Chain and Florey, based on Fleming's work

cards.q: Synthetic drugs appearing early in the 20th century: examples
cards.a: Barbiturates and local anaesthetics

cards.q: X-ray crystallography pioneers (mid-20th century)
cards.a: Hodgkin, Kendrew and Perutz

cards.q: 1980s advance enabling structure-based drug design
cards.a: High-resolution 3D protein structures from crystallography, plus computers

cards.q: Structure-based drug design (SBDD): principle
cards.a: Target 3D structure guides design of tight-binding ligands

cards.q: Biotechnology drugs since the 1980s: main classes
cards.a: Antibodies, enzymes and regulatory proteins (hormones, growth factors, cytokines)

cards.q: How biopharmaceuticals are produced
cards.a: Genetic engineering rather than synthetic chemistry

cards.q: Why modern new drugs are 'invented' rather than discovered
cards.a: Only a fraction come from nature; most are new compounds optimised by design and testing

cards.q: Early drug discovery before knowledge of targets
cards.a: Serendipitous observation of effects of plant extracts or chemicals

cards.q: Indomethacin: how it was found
cards.a: Testing compounds in whole organisms, before any target was known

cards.q: Pharmacology is now defined by
cards.a: Its purpose: what drugs do to organisms and how effects are applied therapeutically

cards.q: First US drug law, and year
cards.a: Federal Pure Food and Drugs Act, 1906

cards.q: What the 1906 Act regulated
cards.a: Interstate transport of adulterated or misbranded foods and drugs

cards.q: Obligations under the 1906 Act for efficacy or safety
cards.a: None

cards.q: Elixir sulfanilamide: solvent and consequence
cards.a: Sulfanilamide in diethylene glycol; over 100 children died

cards.q: 1938 amendment: what new drugs had to show, and who enforced it
cards.a: Safety (not efficacy); enforced by the FDA

cards.q: Before promotion and distribution, a new drug needed
cards.a: Approved New Drug Application (NDA)

cards.q: Thalidomide disaster: years
Thalidomide: use, and defect it caused when taken in early pregnancy
cards.a: Sedative and anti-morning-sickness drug; phocomelia (seal-like limbs)

cards.q: How the thalidomide-defect link was confirmed
cards.a: Epidemiological studies; drug banned worldwide

cards.q: Thalidomide's later use
cards.a: Restricted use as adjuvant in cancer chemotherapy

cards.q: Harris-Kefauver amendments: year and new requirement
cards.a: 1962; proof of efficacy plus documented relative safety (risk-benefit)

cards.q: Acceptable risk in a risk-benefit judgment depends on
cards.a: Seriousness of the disease: the more serious, the greater the acceptable risk

cards.q: Bayh-Dole Act: year and effect
cards.a: 1980; encouraged entrepreneurial drug invention by federally funded academic scientists

cards.q: US biosimilar pathway: law and year
cards.a: Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act, 2010 (part of the Affordable Care Act)

cards.q: Four main kinds of protein drug targets: list
cards.a: Receptors, enzymes, carrier molecules (transporters), ion channels

cards.q: Colchicine (gout): non-receptor target
cards.a: Tubulin, a structural protein

cards.q: Ciclosporin: target
cards.a: Cytosolic immunophilins

cards.q: Drugs that act directly on DNA: class examples
cards.a: Many antimicrobial and antitumour drugs; mutagens and carcinogens

cards.q: Bisphosphonates: target and effect on osteoclasts
cards.a: Bind calcium salts in bone matrix; toxic to osteoclasts

cards.q: Aspirin: enzyme target and type of binding
cards.a: Cyclo-oxygenase; irreversible

cards.q: Enalapril: how it becomes active
cards.a: Esterases convert it to enalaprilat, which inhibits ACE

cards.q: Fluorouracil: false-substrate mechanism
cards.a: Replaces uracil in the pathway but cannot form thymidylate; blocks DNA synthesis

cards.q: Paracetamol: mechanism of liver damage
cards.a: Enzymic conversion to a reactive metabolite

cards.q: Cocaine: transporter it blocks
cards.a: Monoamine neurotransmitter uptake into nerve terminals

cards.q: Tricyclic antidepressants: main target and typical side effect
cards.a: Monoamine transporters; dry mouth from blocking other receptors

cards.q: Symport and antiport
cards.a: Organic molecule moves with Na+ (symport) or opposite to it (antiport)

cards.q: ABC transporters: energy source and examples
cards.a: ATP hydrolysis; Na+-K+ ATPase and multidrug resistance (MDR) transporters

cards.q: MDR transporters: what they do
cards.a: Eject cytotoxic drugs from cancer and microbial cells, causing resistance

cards.q: On-target vs off-target side effects
cards.a: On-target: same receptor as the desired effect; off-target: a different mechanism

cards.q: Opioid constipation and respiratory depression are which type of side effect
cards.a: On-target

cards.q: Why side effects appear as dose rises
cards.a: Higher doses reach targets other than the principal one; no drug is fully specific

cards.q: Drugs that act without binding to a tissue constituent: list
cards.a: Osmotic diuretics, osmotic purgatives, antacids, heavy metal chelating agents

cards.q: Angiotensin: tissues it acts on strongly
cards.a: Vascular smooth muscle and kidney tubule

cards.q: Angiotensin with L-to-D amino acid change
cards.a: Inactive; receptor fails to bind the altered form

cards.q: Imatinib: target and disease
cards.a: Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase; chronic myelogenous leukaemia

cards.q: Statins: enzyme target
cards.a: HMG-CoA reductase

cards.q: Beta-lactam antibiotics: targets
cards.a: Enzymes in bacterial cell-wall synthesis

cards.q: Albuterol: receptor it activates and where
cards.a: Beta-2 adrenergic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, mimicking adrenaline

cards.q: Four receptor superfamilies: list
cards.a: Ligand-gated ion channels; GPCRs; kinase-linked and related receptors; nuclear receptors

cards.q: Type 1 receptors: other name and typical mediators
cards.a: Ionotropic receptors; fast neurotransmitters

cards.q: Type 2 receptors: other names
cards.a: Metabotropic, 7-transmembrane (serpentine, heptahelical) receptors

cards.q: GPCRs: rank by size and main effector link
cards.a: Largest receptor family; coupled mainly via a G protein

cards.q: Number of human GPCRs; share of genome; odorant receptors
cards.a: 865; 1.6% of genome; nearly 500 are odorant receptors

cards.q: Type 3 receptors: basic structure
cards.a: Single transmembrane helix linking extracellular ligand domain to intracellular domain

cards.q: Cytokine receptors vs growth-factor kinase receptors
cards.a: Cytokine receptors lack intracellular kinase and bind cytosolic kinases

cards.q: Pattern-recognition receptors in type 3: examples
cards.a: Toll-like receptors, RIG-I-like receptors, NOD-like receptors

cards.q: Type 4 receptors: function
cards.a: Ligand-activated regulators of gene transcription

cards.q: Timescale of fast synaptic transmission receptor effects
cards.a: Milliseconds

cards.q: Timescale of catecholamine vs thyroid and steroid hormone effects
cards.a: Seconds for catecholamines; hours to days for thyroid and steroid hormones

cards.q: Typical ligand-gated channel subunit count and membrane segments
cards.a: Four or five subunits; 16-20 membrane-spanning segments

cards.q: Sources of receptor subtype diversity
cards.a: Different genes; alternative mRNA splicing; mRNA editing

cards.q: Cloned receptors: how many, from which families
cards.a: Several hundred, from all four structural families

cards.q: Orphan receptor
cards.a: Cloned receptor whose endogenous ligand is unknown

cards.q: How the first receptor clones were obtained
cards.a: Amino-acid sequence of purified receptor, deduced mRNA, cDNA library

cards.q: Cloning strategies that need no purified receptor
cards.a: Expression cloning and sequence-homology cloning

cards.q: Decade receptors became biochemical realities
cards.a: 1970s, through receptor-labelling techniques

cards.q: Why engineered cell lines expressing cloned receptors are used
cards.a: Precise control of receptors; human receptors often differ from animal ones

cards.q: Steroid receptors: location before ligand binding
cards.a: Cytoplasm; translocate to nucleus after binding ligand

cards.q: Hormones acting like steroids via nuclear receptors: list
cards.a: Oestrogen, glucocorticoids, thyroid hormone T3, vitamin D, retinoic acid (vitamin A)

cards.q: Retinoid X receptor (RXR): first described when, and its partner ligand
cards.a: 1990s; binds 9-cis retinoic acid

cards.q: Share of nuclear receptors that are orphans
cards.a: About 40%

cards.q: Human nuclear receptors: number and share of prescription drugs they affect
cards.a: At least 48; about 10-15% of prescription drugs

cards.q: Nuclear receptor ligands and possible activities
cards.a: Mostly small hydrophobic molecules; agonist, antagonist or inverse agonist

cards.q: Nuclear receptors: molecular weight and structure
cards.a: Monomeric proteins of 50-100 kDa

cards.q: DNA-binding domain of nuclear receptors
cards.a: Two zinc fingers in a conserved core

cards.q: Nuclear receptor hinge region role
cards.a: Allows dimerisation and regulates trafficking

cards.q: Nuclear receptor C-terminal domain and AF2
cards.a: Ligand-binding module; AF2 needed for ligand-dependent activation

cards.q: AF1 (N-terminal) activation site role
cards.a: Binds cell-specific transcription factors; works with AF2 when ligand is present

cards.q: Hormone response elements (HREs): length and arrangement
cards.a: Short DNA sequences of about 4-6 base pairs, as pairs or half-sites

cards.q: Nuclear receptor superfamily: drug-metabolism link
cards.a: They regulate expression of drug-metabolising enzymes and transporters

cards.q: Constitutive receptor activity
cards.a: Receptor active even with no ligand bound

cards.q: First GPCR shown to be constitutively active
cards.a: Opioid receptors

cards.q: Receptors with constitutive activity: examples
cards.a: Benzodiazepine, cannabinoid and serotonin receptors; histamine H3 in vivo

cards.q: Inverse agonist definition
cards.a: Ligand that reduces constitutive activation; negative efficacy

cards.q: Neutral antagonist on constitutive activity; its effect on agonists and inverse agonists
cards.a: No effect on basal activity; blocks both agonists and inverse agonists

cards.q: Where inverse agonism was first observed
cards.a: Benzodiazepine receptor

cards.q: Most clinically used receptor antagonists are, in constitutive systems
cards.a: Inverse agonists

cards.q: Two-state model: the two receptor states
cards.a: Resting (R) and activated (R*), in equilibrium

cards.q: Two-state model: agonist, inverse agonist and neutral antagonist affinities
cards.a: Agonist higher for R*; inverse agonist higher for R; neutral antagonist equal

cards.q: Two-state model: how selectivity for R* sets full vs partial agonism
cards.a: Very large R* preference gives full agonist; modest (5-10-fold) gives partial

cards.q: Limitation of the two-state model
cards.a: Receptors have more than two conformations, so simple two-state view is incomplete

cards.q: Biased agonism definition
cards.a: Agonists at one receptor site favour different responses by stabilising different active states

cards.q: Biased agonism examples
cards.a: Ligands at angiotensin receptors; inverse agonists at adrenoceptors

cards.q: RAMPs: year discovered and what they are
cards.a: 1998; membrane proteins that associate with some GPCRs and alter their pharmacology

cards.q: CGRP receptor: composition and why
cards.a: CRLR (inactive alone) plus RAMP1

cards.q: CRLR plus RAMP2 is activated by
cards.a: Adrenomedulin

cards.q: RAMPs mainly associate with which receptor class; exception
cards.a: Class B peptide receptors; calcium-sensing receptor is the exception

cards.q: Arrestin-mediated GPCR signalling: point
cards.a: Works without G proteins; can activate the MAP kinase cascade

cards.q: Old 'one gene, one protein, one G protein, one response' dogma: what challenges it
cards.a: Splicing and editing, receptor association (RAMPs), biased agonism, G-protein-independent signalling

cards.q: Spare receptors (receptor reserve)
cards.a: Receptor pool larger than needed for a full response

cards.q: Receptor occupancy needed for a maximal response with a full agonist (spare receptors)
cards.a: Often less than 1%

cards.q: Economic benefit of spare receptors
cards.a: Same response at lower hormone or transmitter concentration

cards.q: Efficacy (Stephenson): definition
cards.a: Tendency of the drug-receptor complex to adopt the active rather than resting state

cards.q: Full agonist: definition
cards.a: Produces maximal tissue response with less than full receptor occupancy

cards.q: Partial agonist: definition
cards.a: Submaximal response even when all receptors are occupied

cards.q: Intrinsic efficacy vs tissue-dependent efficacy
cards.a: Intrinsic: drug property; tissue: receptor number and coupling efficiency

cards.q: Can 'partial agonist' be used as a general label for a drug
cards.a: No; it applies only to a specific tissue or cell type

cards.q: Buprenorphine in heroin users: why it reduces overdose
cards.a: Weak partial agonist that antagonises heroin at receptors

cards.q: Reversible competitive antagonism: effect on agonist curve
cards.a: Parallel right shift; slope and maximum unchanged; surmountable

cards.q: Dose ratio vs antagonist concentration (reversible competitive)
cards.a: Linear relationship

cards.q: Irreversible competitive antagonism: why it is insurmountable
cards.a: Antagonist does not dissociate, so higher agonist cannot restore occupancy

cards.q: Irreversible enzyme inhibitors used clinically: examples
cards.a: Aspirin, omeprazole, monoamine oxidase inhibitors

cards.q: Allosteric modulator: definition
cards.a: Binds a site other than the agonist site; alters agonist affinity or efficacy, or activates directly

cards.q: Allosteric facilitators: examples
cards.a: Glycine at NMDA receptors; benzodiazepines at GABA-A; cinacalcet at Ca2+ receptor

cards.q: Why allosteric ligands can give subtype selectivity
cards.a: Orthosteric sites are similar across families (e.g. muscarinic), allosteric sites vary more

cards.q: Specific binding: defining property
cards.a: Saturable, because receptors are finite

cards.q: Binding parameters from a saturation curve
cards.a: K (affinity) and Bmax (receptor density)

cards.q: Why agonist binding curves show two receptor populations
cards.a: Receptors exist free or coupled to a G protein; antagonists do not show this

cards.q: Radioligands commonly used
cards.a: Tritium (3H), carbon-14 (14C), iodine-125 (125I)

cards.q: Denervation and receptor number
cards.a: Receptor number increases (denervation supersensitivity)

cards.q: Receptor number with prolonged activation vs absence of agonist
cards.a: Falls with prolonged activation; rises when agonist is absent or scarce

cards.q: Desensitisation vs tachyphylaxis
cards.a: Synonyms; develop within minutes

cards.q: Tolerance: how it differs from desensitisation
cards.a: Gradual loss over hours, days or weeks

cards.q: Mechanisms of loss of drug response: list
cards.a: Change in receptors; translocation; mediator exhaustion; faster metabolic degradation; active extrusion of drug

cards.q: GPCR desensitisation: mechanism
cards.a: Phosphorylation by GPCR kinases, then internalisation of the receptor

cards.q: Ligand-gated channel desensitisation: speed
cards.a: Often rapid and pronounced; conformational change with tight agonist binding

cards.q: Drug resistance (loss of effect): applies to which drugs
cards.a: Antimicrobial and antitumour drugs

cards.q: Myasthenia gravis: mechanism
cards.a: Autoantibodies inactivate nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

cards.q: Thyroid hypersecretion: autoantibody effect
cards.a: Activates thyrotropin (TSH) receptors

cards.q: Inherited GPCR mutations: vasopressin and ACTH receptors
cards.a: Resistance to these hormones

cards.q: LH receptor activating mutation: effect
cards.a: Precocious puberty

cards.q: Beta-2 adrenoceptor polymorphisms: associations
cards.a: Reduced efficacy of beta-agonists in asthma; poor prognosis in heart failure

cards.q: Ligand-gated channels: classed as receptors because
cards.a: Agonist binding is needed to open them

cards.q: Voltage-gated channels: what gates them
cards.a: Changes in transmembrane potential

cards.q: Ways drugs act on ion channels: list
cards.a: Direct binding (orthosteric, allosteric or pore block); indirect via G proteins; altered surface expression

cards.q: Benzodiazepines: channel and site
cards.a: GABA-A chloride channel, allosteric site; facilitate GABA opening

cards.q: Dihydropyridine vasodilators: channel and effect
cards.a: Inhibit opening of L-type calcium channels

cards.q: Local anaesthetics: mechanism on voltage-gated sodium channel
cards.a: Physically plug the channel and block ion permeation

cards.q: Gabapentin: effect on calcium channels
cards.a: Reduces insertion of neuronal calcium channels into the membrane

cards.q: Cys-loop (pentameric) ligand-gated channel family: list
cards.a: Nicotinic acetylcholine, GABA-A, glycine, 5-HT3 receptors

cards.q: Ionotropic glutamate receptors: structure
cards.a: Tetramers; pore built from loops rather than helices

cards.q: P2X receptors: structure
cards.a: Trimers; two transmembrane domains per subunit

cards.q: Cys-loop receptors: subunit arrangement and agonist sites
cards.a: Pentamers with two agonist sites; both must be occupied to open

cards.q: First ion channel cloned, and when
cards.a: Voltage-gated sodium channel, mid-1980s

cards.q: Typical ion channel architecture
cards.a: Often four domains, each with two to six membrane-spanning helices

cards.q: Voltage sensor of voltage-gated channels
cards.a: Helix rich in basic amino acids; moves outward on depolarisation to open channel

cards.q: Voltage-gated channel inactivation
cards.a: Intracellular appendage plugs the channel from inside

cards.q: Voltage-gated Na+ and Ca2+ channel: how built
cards.a: Single large protein with four six-helix domains

cards.q: Potassium channels: number of human subtypes and status
cards.a: More than 70 subtypes; the most numerous and heterogeneous class

cards.q: Inward rectifier K+ channels: helices per subunit
cards.a: Two

cards.q: Two-pore domain K+ channels: feature
cards.a: Each subunit has two P loops

cards.q: ATP-gated K+ channel partner and drug link
cards.a: Sulfonylurea receptor (SUR); sulfonylureas act through it

cards.q: Intracellular Ca2+ effect on channels
cards.a: Opens some K+ and Cl- channels; inactivates voltage-gated Ca2+ channels

cards.q: Intracellular ATP effect on ATP-gated K+ channels
cards.a: Closes them; they are sulfonylurea-sensitive

cards.q: cAMP and cGMP effect on channels
cards.a: Activate channels permeable to Ca2+ and Na+, or to K+

cards.q: Indirect channel modulation by GPCRs
cards.a: Second messenger kinases phosphorylate residues on the channel, altering opening

cards.q: TRPV1 channel: activators
cards.a: Capsaicin, protons when tissue pH falls, and heat

cards.q: Ion channel selectivity set by
cards.a: Pore size and lining; cation or anion selective

cards.q: Store-operated channels open when
cards.a: Intracellular Ca2+ stores are depleted

cards.q: IP3 and ryanodine receptors: location and role
cards.a: Endoplasmic or sarcoplasmic reticulum; release Ca2+ from stores

cards.q: ATP-sensitive K+ channels open when
cards.a: Intracellular ATP falls (cell short of energy)

cards.q: Voltage-gated channel types: which ions are carried by voltage-gated channels
cards.a: Na+, K+ and Ca2+

cards.q: Meaning of 'ayurveda'
cards.a: 'Science of life' in Sanskrit

cards.q: Ayurvedic texts describing plant pharmacology: names and plant count
cards.a: Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas; more than 700 plants

cards.q: Contribution of Indian Ayurveda and Chinese plant systems to new medicines
cards.a: Strong philosophical and experiential base; ayurveda also has an experimental basis

cards.q: Sir Ram Nath Chopra: known as
cards.a: Father of Indian pharmacology

cards.q: First centre for pharmacology study and research in India: where
cards.a: Calcutta School of Tropical Medicine

cards.q: Chair Chopra held at that centre
cards.a: Professor of Pharmacology including Indigenous Drugs

cards.q: Reverse pharmacology: starting point
cards.a: Clinically documented effects of a traditional remedy, then laboratory study

cards.q: Who introduced reverse pharmacology for Ayurvedic drugs in India
cards.a: Chopra and Sen

cards.q: Sen and Bose 1931: Rauwolfia serpentina finding
cards.a: Antihypertensive and tranquillising effects

cards.q: Indian Act regulating import, manufacture and distribution of drugs
cards.a: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940

cards.q: Drugs and Cosmetics Act section 17B: what it empowers
cards.a: Inspect, seize and confiscate adulterated or spurious drugs

cards.q: Body authorising import or manufacture of a new drug, orphan drugs included
cards.a: CDSCO (Central Drugs Standard Control Organization)

cards.q: Year India joined the WHO Programme for International Drug Monitoring
Body that manages the WHO drug monitoring programme
cards.a: Uppsala Monitoring Centre, Sweden

cards.q: India's national centre for WHO drug monitoring
cards.a: Department of Pharmacology, AIIMS, New Delhi

cards.q: Three purinergic receptor families
cards.a: Adenosine (P1, G protein), P2Y (GPCR), P2X (ion channel)

cards.q: Purinergic receptor family that is a ligand-gated ion channel
cards.a: P2X (P2X1 to P2X7)

cards.q: Platelet ADP receptor targeted by antiplatelet drugs
cards.a: P2Y12

cards.q: Prodrugs that block platelet P2Y12
cards.a: Clopidogrel, prasugrel

cards.q: Allosteric P2Y12 antagonists
cards.a: Ticagrelor, cangrelor

cards.q: Non-selective blocker of many P2X and P2Y receptors
cards.a: Suramin

cards.q: Methylxanthines that block adenosine receptors
cards.a: Caffeine, theophylline

cards.q: Selective A2A agonist used in cardiac diagnostic tests
cards.a: Regadenoson

cards.q: G protein classes of pharmacological importance: list
cards.a: Gs, Gi, Go, Gq, G12/13

cards.q: Gs effect
cards.a: Stimulates adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP

cards.q: Gi effect
cards.a: Inhibits adenylyl cyclase, lowering cAMP

cards.q: Gq effect
cards.a: Activates phospholipase C: IP3 and DAG, Ca2+ release, PKC

cards.q: G12/13 effect
cards.a: Activates Rho and Rho kinase

cards.q: Toxin that keeps Gs active by blocking its GTPase
cards.a: Cholera toxin

cards.q: Toxin that blocks Gi and Go function
cards.a: Pertussis toxin

cards.q: Step that terminates G protein alpha-subunit signalling
cards.a: Hydrolysis of GTP to GDP by its own GTPase

cards.q: Cardiac receptors with opposite effects via different G proteins
cards.a: M2 muscarinic and beta-1 adrenoceptors

cards.q: Chemical antagonism: examples
cards.a: Dimercaprol binding heavy metals; infliximab sequestering TNF

cards.q: Pharmacokinetic antagonism example
cards.a: Phenytoin speeding warfarin metabolism lowers its anticoagulant effect

cards.q: Physiological antagonism example
cards.a: Histamine raises gastric acid; omeprazole blocks the proton pump

cards.q: Non-competitive block downstream of receptor: examples
cards.a: Ketamine in NMDA channel; verapamil and nifedipine blocking Ca2+ entry

cards.q: Types of drug antagonism: list
cards.a: Chemical, pharmacokinetic, competitive (reversible or irreversible), block of receptor-response linkage, physiological

cards.q: Step governed by affinity; step governed by efficacy
cards.a: Binding (occupation); activation

cards.q: Efficacy of a simple antagonist
cards.a: Zero

cards.q: Black (1970): second histamine receptor class proposed for gastric secretion
cards.a: H2 receptor

cards.q: Body that convenes agreed receptor classifications
cards.a: IUPHAR expert working groups

cards.q: Captopril: enzyme and type of inhibition
cards.a: Angiotensin-converting enzyme; competitive (substrate analogue)

cards.q: Na+ channel blockers named in R&D: list
cards.a: Tetrodotoxin, saxitoxin, local anaesthetics, phenytoin, antidysrhythmics

cards.q: Agents that block Na+ channel inactivation: list
cards.a: Veratridine, batrachotoxin, scorpion toxins, DDT, pyrethroids

cards.q: Patch clamp: devised by, and what it measures
cards.a: Neher and Sakmann; current through single ion channels

cards.q: Segments lining the nicotinic receptor pore
